CHAPTER XXXV

Gerard awoke, and found Denys watching him with some anxiety.

“It is you for sleeping! Why, 'tis high noon.”

“It was a blessed sleep,” said Gerard; “methinks Heaven sent it me. It
hath put as it were a veil between me and that awful night. To think
that you and I sit here alive and well. How terrible a dream I seem to
have had!”

“Ay, lad, that is the wise way to look at these things when once they
are past, why, they are dreams, shadows. Break thy fast, and then thou
wilt think no more on't. Moreover, I promised to bring thee on to the
town by noon, and take thee to his worship.”

Gerard then sopped some rye bread in red wine and ate it to break his
fast: then went with Denys over the scene of combat, and came back
shuddering, and finally took the road with his friend, and kept peering
through the hedges, and expecting sudden attacks unreasonably, till they
reached the little town. Denys took him to “The White Hart”.

“No fear of cut-throats here,” said he. “I know the landlord this many
a year. He is a burgess, and looks to be bailiff. 'Tis here I was making
for yestreen. But we lost time, and night o'ertook us--and--

“And you saw a woman at the door, and would be wiser than a Jeanneton;
she told us they were nought.”

“Why, what saved our lives if not a woman? Ay, and risked her own to do
it.”

“That is true, Denys; and though women are nothing to me, I long to
thank this poor girl, and reward her, ay, though I share every doit in
my purse with her. Do not you?”

“Parbleu.”

“Where shall we find her?”

“Mayhap the alderman will tell us. We must go to him first.”

The alderman received them with a most singular and inexplicable
expression of countenance. However, after a moment's reflection, he wore
a grim smile, and finally proceeded to put interrogatories to Gerard,
and took down the answers. This done, he told them that they must
stay in the town till the thieves were tried, and be at hand to give
evidence, on peril of fine and imprisonment. They looked very blank at
this.

“However,” said he, “'twill not be long, the culprits having been taken
red-handed.” He added, “And you know, in any case you could not leave
the place this week.”

Denys stared at this remark, and Gerard smiled at what he thought the
simplicity of the old gentleman in dreaming that a provincial town of
Burgundy had attraction to detain him from Rome and Margaret.

He now went to that which was nearest both their hearts.

“Your worship,” said he, “we cannot find our benefactress in the town.”

“Nay, but who is your benefactress?”

“Who? why the good girl that came to you by night and saved our lives at
peril of her own. Oh sir, our hearts burn within us to thank and bless
her; where is she?”

Gerard woke as one rises from a cauldron that has boiled over in the night and been skimmed at dawn—his mind still filmed, but the worst scum gone. Denys sat near, not dozing, but watching, with that soldier’s vigilance that listens even with the eyes. Through the small casement came the town’s noon—distant hammering on wood, a cart’s iron hoop crying on stone, pigeons clapping and cooing under the eaves; and underneath all, a steady human murmur like a hearth-fire heard from the next room.

“It is you for sleeping!” Denys broke out. “Why, ’tis high noon.”

“It was a blessed sleep,” said Gerard, and his voice surprised him with its steadiness. “Methinks Heaven sent it me. It hath put as it were a veil between me and that awful night. To think that you and I sit here alive and well. How terrible a dream I seem to have had!”

“Ay, lad; that is the wise way to look at these things when once they are past—why, they are dreams, shadows.” Denys nodded toward the table as if that were the proper altar for gratitude. “Break thy fast, and then thou wilt think no more on’t. Moreover, I promised to bring thee on to the town by noon, and take thee to his worship.”

Denys spoke of breakfast as if it were a remedy compounded by old women and proved by generations. Gerard obeyed him with the obedience of a man newly returned to his body. He took coarse rye bread, dark as tilled earth, tore it with his hands, and sopped it in red wine. The wine ran into the bread’s pores, staining it a purplish brown, softening its stubborn grain until it yielded like muscle warmed. He ate—slow at first, then with the simple hunger that comes when fear has at last loosened its grip. The sourness of rye, the fruit and bite of the wine, the faint smell of woodsmoke in the room—these things, homely and exact, stitched him back into daylight.

Then Denys would not let him brood. They went out.

The road beyond the lodging lay innocent enough; birds chattered in the hedgerows as if no human throat had cried there. Yet Gerard’s feet, having learned the night’s lesson, led him unwillingly over the very place where steel had sung. He saw again, with his waking eyes, what his sleep had tried to fold away: trampled grass, a smear of earth where bodies had wrestled, the broken twigs in the ditch. The sounds of noon—children calling somewhere, a dog’s bark, the rhythmic thud of a mallet—did not belong to that patch of ground, and that mismatch made him shudder. It was as if the world had changed its language between one hour and the next, and his memory could not translate.

They turned back, and took the road for the little town. Gerard’s gaze kept slipping to the hedges, as if every green bank hid an ambush; he hated his own unreasonable expectation of sudden hands and knives, but could not lay it down at once. Denys walked with the ease of a man who trusts walls and people more than open fields; he hummed once under his breath, a tune without words, as though to set the air right again.

At length the houses gathered, close-shouldered, the street narrowing into a throat that swallowed hoofbeats and spat them back in echoes. The town had its own music: the clink of a blacksmith’s tools, a churn of voices in a market nook, the splash of water poured from a pail. Compared with the wild silence of the road, it was a kind of safety. Noise, here, was not menace but proof—proof of hearths tended, of loaves baked, of lives continuing.

Denys led him straight to an inn whose sign creaked gently: The White Hart. From within came the warm breath of men and cooking—yeast and ale, fat meeting flame, onions sweating down in a pot. A woman’s laugh rose, then was swallowed by the room’s general rumble.

“No fear of cut-throats here,” said Denys, with a confidence born of familiarity. “I know the landlord this many a year. He is a burgess, and looks to be bailiff. ’Tis here I was making for yestreen. But we lost time, and night o’ertook us—and—”

“And you saw a woman at the door, and would be wiser than a Jeanneton; she told us they were nought,” Gerard finished, unable to keep the tartness from his tone.

Denys’s eyebrows lifted, then lowered as if in honest shame. “Why, what saved our lives if not a woman? Ay, and risked her own to do it.”

“That is true, Denys.” Gerard’s chest tightened, not with fear now, but with a fierce, almost childlike gratitude that demanded a shape, a name, a face. “And though women are nothing to me, I long to thank this poor girl, and reward her—ay, though I share every doit in my purse with her. Do not you?”

“Parbleu.”

“Where shall we find her?”

“Mayhap the alderman will tell us. We must go to him first.”

So they went to the alderman—through streets that smelled of damp stone and stale straw, past a baker’s where hot crust breathed out into the air, past a yard where someone split kindling with measured strokes that sounded, to Gerard’s startled nerves, like blows. In each tongue he heard in the street—Burgundian turns, French clipped by trade, words thrown quick between neighbors—there was that hidden power of a place: the way a town speaks can make a stranger feel either invited or judged. Gerard, who carried other sounds within him and other names for bread and wine and mercy, felt the edges of his own speech press against theirs.

The alderman received them with a most singular and inexplicable expression of countenance. It was not displeasure exactly, nor welcome; rather the look of a man who has tasted something and cannot decide whether it is sweet or spoiled. He studied them as though the two travelers had walked in carrying a story already half-known to him.

However, after a moment’s reflection, he let a grim smile creep over his mouth, like a knife slid back into its sheath. Then he began to question Gerard closely—where they had come from, what hour they had been set upon, how many assailants, what weapons, what words were spoken. He wrote down the answers with careful strokes, as exact as a cook measuring spices that might, misjudged, ruin the whole dish.

When he had done, he looked up and said in a tone that made law sound as everyday as buying salt: they must stay in the town till the thieves were tried, and be at hand to give evidence, on peril of fine and imprisonment.

They looked very blank at that; Denys’s mouth opened a little, then shut. Gerard thought of Rome and of Margaret as of a loaf left half-baked—time and heat required, but now interrupted; his impatience rose like yeast.

“However,” the alderman added, as if offering a small sweet after a bitter draught, “’twill not be long, the culprits having been taken red-handed.”

Then, with that same odd gleam in his eye, he said, “And you know, in any case you could not leave the place this week.”

Denys stared at this remark, his face hardening in puzzlement. Gerard, thinking the old gentleman’s provincial mind had made a harmless jest, smiled—smiled at the simplicity of dreaming that a little town in Burgundy could detain him from Rome and Margaret, as if the world’s great fire burned no hotter than their own small hearth.

But what lay nearest both their hearts was not Rome at that instant, nor even freedom. It was the memory of a girl in the dark, the sudden brave voice that had bent danger aside.

“Your worship,” said Gerard, and the words came out with a warmth that surprised even him, “we cannot find our benefactress in the town.”

“Nay,” said the alderman, “but who is your benefactress?”

“Who?” Gerard leaned forward, the room’s sounds falling away as if a door had closed on them. “Why, the good girl that came to you by night and saved our lives at peril of her own. Oh sir, our hearts burn within us to thank and bless her; where is she?”
